Virological Response and Monitoring for Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Individuals with cirrhosis should undergo screening for hepatocellular carcinoma every six months using ultrasound or alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) testing. This is critical for early detection and management. 2. Treatment of Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) in Adolescents (12–17 years): For genotypes 1, 4, 5, and 6, a 12-week course of sofosbuvir/ledipasvir is recommended. For genotype 2, a 12-week course of sofosbuvir/ribavirin is advised. For genotype 3, a 24-week course of sofosbuvir/ribavirin is required. 3. HCV Treatment in Adults Without Cirrhosis: A 12-week regimen of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, sofosbuvir/daclatasvir, or an 8-week course of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir is recommended. 4. HCV Treatment in Adults with Compensated Cirrhosis: A 12-week regimen of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir or glecaprevir/pibrentasvir is recommended. For sofosbuvir/daclatasvir, treatment duration depends on prior therapy and genotype, ranging from 12 to 24 weeks. 5. Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) Vaccination and Prevention: Universal infant and perinatal HBV vaccination is essential to prevent mother-to-child transmission and control the HBV epidemic. However, less than half of countries implement timely birth-dose vaccination. Adults living with HIV are at higher risk of HBV infection. All newly diagnosed HIV patients should be screened for HBV markers (HBsAg and anti-HBs) and vaccinated if non-immune. People living with HIV may have a reduced response to the HBV vaccine, especially those with low CD4 counts. A four-dose schedule of double-strength vaccine (40 µg) may be more effective. 6. HBV Treatment in HIV Co-infection: HIV co-infection accelerates HBV progression, leading to higher risks of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality. Therefore, all HIV patients should be screened for HBV and treated if necessary. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), combined with lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC), is the preferred treatment for both HIV and HBV co-infection. This combination suppresses HBV replication, reverses liver damage, and reduces HBV-related mortality. Abrupt discontinuation of TDF or 3TC can lead to HBV reactivation and liver flares, so treatment should be carefully managed. 7. Testing for Chronic HBV and HCV: Routine HBV testing is recommended for all adults and adolescents in regions with ≥2% or ≥5% HBsAg prevalence. Testing should be linked to prevention, care, and treatment services. Pregnant women should be routinely tested for HBV (HBsAg) during antenatal care, especially in high-prevalence settings. 8. Malaria and HIV Co-infection: People living with HIV are at increased risk of severe malaria and malaria-related mortality. Intermittent preventive treatment during pregnancy and seasonal malaria chemoprophylaxis are recommended in high-transmission areas. However, sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine should not be used in individuals taking co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. Prompt and effective antimalarial treatment is critical for people living with HIV who develop malaria. Parasitological confirmation should be performed, but treatment should not be delayed if diagnosis is unavailable. 9. Buruli Ulcer and HIV Co-infection: Buruli ulcer, caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, is more common in individuals with HIV, particularly those with low CD4 counts. HIV may increase the severity of Buruli ulcer lesions. Diagnosis is typically clinical but can be confirmed using PCR, direct smear examination, or histopathology. Treatment involves an 8-week course of rifampicin combined with clarithromycin or moxifloxacin. For individuals on dolutegravir (DTG)-based antiretroviral therapy (ART), the DTG dose should be increased due to interactions with rifampicin. Rapid ART initiation is recommended for all individuals co-infected with Buruli ulcer and HIV, alongside screening for tuberculosis (TB) and other opportunistic infections. 10. Leishmaniasis and HIV Co-infection: Leishmaniasis, caused by Leishmania parasites, disproportionately affects marginalized populations. The burden of visceral leishmaniasis among people living with HIV has increased in recent decades. Effective management requires early diagnosis and treatment, as well as integration with HIV care services. This detailed explanation provides a comprehensive understanding of the recommendations and considerations for managing HBV, HCV, malaria, Buruli ulcer, and leishmaniasis, particularly in the context of HIV co-infection.
